faq.a: No, AIDS is defined by CD4 <200 cells/µL or an AIDS‑defining illness.
faq.q: Can a patient with a CD4 count of 250 cells/µL have AIDS?

faq.a: It prevents Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and several bacterial infections common in low CD4 counts.
Treat any life‑threatening opportunistic infection first, then arrange referral for ART as soon as possible.
faq.q: What is the first step if ART is unavailable?

exam: A 32‑year‑old woman with weight loss and chronic cough tests HIV‑positive; CD4 is 180 cells/µL. What is the next immediate management step? — Start ART after initiating TB treatment, give cotrimoxazole prophylaxis, and arrange baseline labs.
How does WHO clinical staging help in a district hospital without CD4 testing? — It guides when to start ART and prophylaxis based on observable opportunistic infections.

A patient on ART presents with new fever and headache; CSF shows India‑ink positive organisms. Which condition is most likely and how is it treated? — Cryptococcal meningitis; treat with amphotericin B plus flucytosine induction, then fluconazole consolidation.
Why is efavirenz avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy? — It is teratogenic; dolutegravir is preferred after the first trimester.
What distinguishes pulmonary TB from Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia on chest X‑ray? — TB shows focal infiltrates or cavitation; PCP shows diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates.
A patient with HIV presents with oral thrush but CD4 count is 350 cells/µL. Does this meet AIDS criteria? — No, oral thrush alone is not an AIDS‑defining illness; monitor and treat locally.
Explain why cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is continued even after CD4 rises above 200 cells/µL. — Guidelines recommend continuation for at least 6 months after immune recovery to prevent relapse.
In a low‑resource setting, how would you screen for cryptococcal disease without CrAg testing? — Perform a lumbar puncture with India‑ink staining if meningitis symptoms are present.
ai.title: Acquired Immunodeficiency Syndrome (AIDS)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: AIDS is the advanced stage of HIV infection, defined by severe CD4 depletion or AIDS‑defining illnesses. Diagnosis relies on serology and CD4 count, with staging guiding management in low‑resource settings.

b: HIV antibody/antigen rapid test confirms infection
CD4 count quantifies immune suppression
Viral load, if available, assesses treatment response
sections.p: AIDS is diagnosed when a person with HIV has a CD4 count <200 cells/µL or presents with one or more AIDS‑defining conditions.

t.b: Is the patient infected with HIV? – Positive indicates infection; negative requires repeat after window period.
How severe is immunosuppression? – <200 cells/µL meets AIDS criteria; 200‑349 is advanced HIV.

t.a: Screen for AIDS‑defining illnesses (e.g., TB, cryptococcal meningitis)
t.b: Does the patient have an opportunistic infection? – Presence confirms AIDS regardless of CD4.

b: Stage 1: Asymptomatic or mild mucocutaneous manifestations
Stage 2: Moderate weight loss, recurrent oral ulcers
Stage 3: Pulmonary TB, severe bacterial infections
Stage 4: Kaposi sarcoma, cryptococcal meningitis, CD4 <200
sections.p: The WHO clinical staging system (Stages 1‑4) is used where CD4 testing is scarce; Stage 4 corresponds to AIDS.

b: Unprotected heterosexual intercourse – most common in East Africa
Sharing of injection equipment
Perinatal transmission
Blood transfusion with unscreened products
sections.p: AIDS results from uncontrolled replication of HIV, a retrovirus transmitted primarily by sexual contact, contaminated needles, or mother‑to‑child transmission.

b: Profound, unexplained weight loss (>10% body weight)
Chronic diarrhoea (>2 weeks) with malabsorption
Recurrent oral thrush or ulceration
Pulmonary TB symptoms (cough, night sweats, haemoptysis)
Neurological signs: focal deficits, seizures (cryptococcal meningitis)
sections.p: Patients may present with chronic weight loss, persistent fever, diarrhoea, or an AIDS‑defining opportunistic infection.
Prioritise tests that confirm HIV status, assess immune function, and identify opportunistic infections.

t.b: Is there pulmonary TB or Kaposi sarcoma? – Infiltrates suggest TB; nodular lesions may indicate Kaposi.
Does the patient have Mycobacterium tuberculosis? – Positive confirms TB; guides therapy.
Is cryptococcal meningitis present? – Positive in blood or CSF indicates infection.
Is there anaemia or cytopenia? – Low haemoglobin may reflect chronic disease or marrow involvement.

b: Acute respiratory failure from TB or Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
Altered mental status with meningitis
Severe diarrhoea leading to dehydration and electrolyte loss
Unexplained high fever >38.5 °C for >48 h
sections.p: Rapid deterioration signals life‑threatening opportunistic disease.

b: First‑line ART: Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir – potent, low toxicity, once‑daily.
Avoid efavirenz in pregnancy (use dolutegravir after first trimester).
TB treatment: Rifampicin‑based regimen – start ART 2 weeks after TB therapy if CD4 <50, otherwise after 8 weeks.
Cryptococcal meningitis: Amphotericin B + flucytosine induction, then fluconazole consolidation.
Primary prophylaxis: Cotrimoxazole for CD4 <200 to prevent Pneumocystis and bacterial infections.
sections.p: Start antiretroviral therapy (ART) as soon as possible, treat opportunistic infections, and provide prophylaxis.

b: Clinic visit every 3 months for ART refill and adherence counseling
CD4 count every 6 months; viral load annually where possible
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and seasonal influenza
Educate on safe sex, needle hygiene, and mother‑to‑child transmission prevention
sections.p: Regular monitoring of CD4, viral load (if available), and opportunistic infection screening is essential.

b: Severe protein‑energy malnutrition – low weight but CD4 may be >200
Chronic TB alone – may cause weight loss but does not meet AIDS criteria without CD4 data
sections.p: Advanced HIV infection without AIDS‑defining illnesses and severe malnutrition can mimic AIDS.

b: CD4 count can be transiently higher during acute infections – repeat after stabilization
Rapid HIV test may be negative during the window period – repeat after 4 weeks if exposure recent
sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely normal in early disease or in resource‑limited labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of severe dyspnoea or chest pain
New focal neurological deficits or seizures
